text: When Krakatoa erupted in 1883, people heard it almost five thousand kilometres away.
Within minutes, a column of ash could rise more than thirty kilometres, punching straight through the clouds.
Thousands of strikes, sparked by ash grains rubbing against each other.
Then the column could collapse under its own weight.
Avalanches of glowing ash and gas, hotter than three hundred degrees, would race down the slopes faster than a car on a motorway.
Rain mixes with the fresh ash, thick as wet concrete.
Rivers of mud, called lahars, could roll through the valleys, dragging whole trees along.
And at midday… the sky turns completely black.
But for the rest of the continent, the worst hasn't even arrived.
